notes: Phase 2 dataset expansion. Conservative verdicts. Unknown defaults to VET FIRST. Sources reference ASPCA Poison Control and Michigan State University VDL owner guidance where applicable.

foods.explanation: Chocolate contains methylxanthines that can affect the heart and nervous system of pets.
foods.action: Contact a vet or poison control immediately.
sources: Michigan State University Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory

foods.explanation: Caffeine can overstimulate the heart and nervous system of pets.
foods.action: Contact a vet or poison control immediately.
sources: Michigan State University Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory

foods.explanation: Alcohol can depress the nervous system and cause serious poisoning in pets.
foods.action: Contact a vet or poison control immediately.
sources: Michigan State University Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory

foods.explanation: Raw dough can expand in the stomach and produce alcohol during digestion.
foods.action: Seek veterinary care immediately.
sources: Michigan State University Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory

foods.explanation: Xylitol can cause dangerously low blood sugar and acute liver injury in dogs.
foods.action: Seek veterinary care immediately.

foods.explanation: Grapes and raisins have been associated with sudden kidney injury in dogs.
foods.action: Contact a vet or poison control immediately.
sources: Michigan State University Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory

foods.explanation: Allium vegetables can damage red blood cells and lead to anemia in pets.
foods.action: Avoid feeding and contact a vet if ingestion is suspected.
sources: Michigan State University Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory

foods.explanation: Macadamia nuts can cause weakness, tremors, and other neurologic signs in dogs.
foods.action: Seek veterinary advice promptly.
sources: Michigan State University Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory

foods.explanation: Many nuts are high in fat and oils and may cause digestive upset or pancreatitis depending on amount consumed.
foods.action: Avoid feeding. Contact a vet if vomiting, diarrhea, or lethargy occurs.

foods.explanation: Many pets have limited lactose tolerance and may develop digestive upset after consuming dairy.
foods.action: Avoid feeding. Contact a vet if vomiting, diarrhea, or lethargy occurs.

foods.explanation: Citrus fruits and peels can cause gastrointestinal irritation, and risk depends on amount consumed.
foods.action: Contact a vet if a large amount was eaten or symptoms develop.

foods.explanation: Coconut products may cause digestive upset or diarrhea depending on individual sensitivity and amount.
foods.action: Avoid feeding large amounts. Contact a vet if symptoms occur.

foods.explanation: Risk varies by species and amount, and some parts may cause digestive upset or other concerns.
foods.action: Contact a vet if a meaningful amount was eaten, especially if symptoms appear.
sources: Michigan State University Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory

foods.explanation: Some peanut butter products contain xylitol, which is dangerous for dogs.
foods.action: Check the ingredient label immediately. If xylitol is listed, seek veterinary care.

foods.explanation: Excessive salt intake can lead to gastrointestinal or neurologic effects depending on amount consumed.
foods.action: Contact a vet if a large amount was eaten or symptoms develop.

foods.explanation: Raw or undercooked meat may contain bacteria that can cause illness in pets.
foods.action: Monitor for symptoms and contact a vet if vomiting, diarrhea, or lethargy occurs.

foods.explanation: Raw eggs may carry bacteria and may cause illness depending on exposure and pet health.
foods.action: Contact a vet if gastrointestinal symptoms develop.

foods.explanation: Bones can cause choking, oral injury, or intestinal obstruction depending on size and preparation.
foods.action: Contact a vet promptly if a bone was swallowed or symptoms occur.

foods.explanation: High fat foods may cause digestive upset and can trigger pancreatitis in some pets.
foods.action: Avoid feeding. Contact a vet if vomiting, abdominal pain, or lethargy occurs.

foods.explanation: Spoiled foods may contain toxins or bacteria that can cause illness in pets.
foods.action: Contact a vet if ingestion is suspected or symptoms develop.
sources: Michigan State University Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory

foods.explanation: Plain baked bread is generally less concerning, but ingredients and amount consumed matter.
foods.action: Contact a vet if the product contained toxic ingredients or symptoms occur.

foods.explanation: Risk depends on whether xylitol is present and how much was consumed.
foods.action: Check ingredients immediately. If xylitol is present, seek veterinary care.

foods.explanation: Risk depends on chocolate type, amount consumed, and pet size.
foods.action: Contact a vet or poison control with product details and estimated amount eaten.

foods.explanation: Any raisin-containing food carries kidney risk for dogs, and amount matters.
foods.action: Contact a vet or poison control promptly.

foods.explanation: Seasonings may contain concentrated allium compounds, and risk depends on amount consumed.
foods.action: Contact a vet if more than a small taste was eaten or symptoms occur.

foods.explanation: Peels and oils are more concentrated than fruit and may cause irritation depending on amount.
foods.action: Contact a vet if ingestion is suspected or symptoms develop.

foods.explanation: Desserts containing coconut, sugar, and fat may cause digestive upset depending on amount.
foods.action: Monitor for symptoms and contact a vet if vomiting or diarrhea occurs.

foods.explanation: Lactose and high fat content may cause digestive upset depending on amount and tolerance.
foods.action: Contact a vet if symptoms are significant or persistent.

foods.explanation: Nut mixes may include toxic ingredients such as chocolate, raisins, or macadamia nuts.
foods.action: Identify ingredients and contact a vet if high-risk items were included.

foods.explanation: Excess salt exposure can cause illness depending on the amount consumed.
foods.action: Contact a vet if you suspect significant exposure or symptoms develop.

foods.explanation: Apples are safe for dogs when seeds are removed.
foods.action: Remove seeds and core before feeding.

foods.explanation: Bananas are safe for dogs when plain and unseasoned.
foods.action: Feed in moderation as a treat.

foods.explanation: Plain cooked beef without bones is safe for dogs.
foods.action: Ensure it is fully cooked and contains no bones or seasonings.

foods.explanation: Blueberries are safe for dogs when plain and unseasoned.
foods.action: Feed in moderation as a treat.

foods.explanation: Broccoli is safe for dogs when plain and unseasoned.
foods.action: Feed in moderation as a treat.

foods.explanation: Cantaloupe is safe for dogs when plain and unseasoned.
foods.action: Remove rind and seeds before feeding.

foods.explanation: Carrots are safe for dogs when plain and unseasoned.
foods.action: Feed raw or cooked without seasonings.

foods.explanation: Cauliflower is safe for dogs when plain and unseasoned.
foods.action: Feed in moderation as a treat.

foods.explanation: Celery is safe for dogs when plain and unseasoned.
foods.action: Feed in moderation as a treat.

foods.explanation: Cheese is safe for dogs in small amounts when plain.
foods.action: Feed only small amounts as an occasional treat.

foods.explanation: Plain cooked chicken without bones is safe for dogs.
foods.action: Ensure it is fully cooked and contains no bones or seasonings.

foods.explanation: Cooked pumpkin is safe for dogs when plain and unseasoned.
foods.action: Feed plain cooked pumpkin without added spices or sugar.

foods.explanation: Green beans are safe for dogs when plain and unseasoned.
foods.action: Feed raw or cooked without seasonings.

foods.explanation: Kiwi is safe for dogs when plain and unseasoned.
foods.action: Remove skin before feeding.

foods.explanation: Xylitol-free peanut butter is safe for dogs in moderation.
foods.action: Verify the product contains no xylitol before feeding.

foods.explanation: Pineapple is safe for dogs when plain and unseasoned.
foods.action: Remove tough outer skin and core before feeding.

foods.explanation: Plain popcorn without salt, butter, or seasonings is safe for dogs.
foods.action: Feed only plain, unseasoned popcorn in moderation.

foods.explanation: Plain cooked pork without bones is safe for dogs.
foods.action: Ensure it is fully cooked and contains no bones or seasonings.

foods.explanation: Strawberries are safe for dogs when plain and unseasoned.
foods.action: Feed in moderation as a treat.

foods.explanation: Plain cooked turkey without bones is safe for dogs.
foods.action: Ensure it is fully cooked and contains no bones or seasonings.
